etymology: From Latin aeternalis "eternal," from aeternus.
biblical_def: The divine attribute that God has neither beginning nor end nor succession of moments — He is the I AM, the Alpha and Omega (Ps 90:2; Rev 1:8).
webster_summary: God's existence without beginning or end.
webster_full: The attribute of God by which He exists without beginning, without end, and without succession; the eternal now in which all moments are present to Him at once.
scriptures: Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord.
For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy.
corruption_summary: Reduced to merely 'a long time' — God lasting forever instead of God transcending time.
corruption_paragraphs: Eternality is not endless time-stretch — it is timelessness. God is not older than the universe; He is outside the river of moments, holding it all in view at once. The mistake makes God a creature with longer batteries; the truth makes Him the I AM.
usage: God's eternality grounds His promises.
He inhabits eternity — that is why His word does not fail.

etymology: Reformed dogmatic term — the call of the gospel that effectively brings the elect to faith.
biblical_def: The inward, sovereign, Spirit-wrought summons that draws the elect from death to life and renders the gospel call effective in them (Rom 8:30; John 6:44).
webster_summary: The inward call of the Spirit that brings to faith.
webster_full: A theological term distinguishing the outward gospel call (universal proclamation) from the inward, irresistible, regenerating summons of the Spirit by which the elect are brought to faith and new birth.
scriptures: Whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified.
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.
We preach Christ crucified... unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God.
corruption_summary: Collapsed into the outward gospel invitation, missing the Spirit's sovereign work of effectual application.
corruption_paragraphs: Many are called outwardly; few are called effectually. The outward call goes out to all; the inward call awakens the dead. Without the second, the first only condemns. Pray for the effectual call as you preach the gospel call.
usage: Preach the gospel call; pray the Spirit's effectual call.
The effectual call cannot be resisted.

etymology: From Old English in + dwellan "to remain."
biblical_def: The personal residence of the Holy Spirit in every believer at conversion, sealing them and uniting them to Christ (Rom 8:9-11; 1 Cor 6:19).
webster_summary: The Spirit's residence in every believer.
webster_full: The personal, permanent residence of the Holy Spirit in every Christian from the moment of saving faith — sealing for the day of redemption, communicating Christ's life, and bearing fruit in the believer.
scriptures: Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?
In whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance.
corruption_summary: Replaced by talk of 'inviting Jesus into your heart' that obscures the precise work of the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: The indwelling is not metaphor. The Spirit personally takes up residence in the believer. He is not a force or influence but the third Person of the Trinity living in His temple. Holy Spirit theology, not just heart-warmth, is what holds believers.
usage: Live as a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Grieve not the Spirit who indwells you.

etymology: From Latin in- (not) + passibilis (capable of suffering).
biblical_def: The classical Christian doctrine that God in His divine nature is not subject to passions imposed from outside Himself — He is not pulled around by emotion in the manner of creatures (Mal 3:6; James 1:17).
webster_summary: God is not pulled by external passions.
webster_full: The doctrine, held by the historic church, that God in His divine nature is not subject to passions or emotional change imposed from outside Himself; He acts always from His own perfect will and not in reaction. He is not unfeeling — He is not vulnerable.
scriptures: For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent.
corruption_summary: Mocked as Stoic stiffness rather than understood as divine sovereignty over emotion.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern theology often rejects impassibility, wanting a 'God who suffers with us.' Classical theology insists God is not pulled around by external causes — He acts in love because He IS love, not because we made Him feel it. The two visions yield very different prayer lives.
usage: God's love is His character, not His reaction.
Recover impassibility to recover His sovereignty.

etymology: Reformed term distinguishing the once-for-all setting-apart from progressive growth.
biblical_def: The decisive break with sin's dominion at conversion — the believer is set apart in Christ, transferred from death to life, no longer a slave of sin (Rom 6:1-14; 1 Cor 6:11).
webster_summary: The decisive break with sin's reign at conversion.
webster_full: The Reformed doctrine that at the moment of saving union with Christ, the believer is decisively set apart unto God — sin's dominion broken, the new man put on, the old man crucified — distinct from progressive sanctification which follows.
scriptures: Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.
By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
corruption_summary: Collapsed entirely into progressive sanctification, missing the once-for-all break that grounds growth.
corruption_paragraphs: Many believers feel sin still wins because they never received the news that the chains are already broken. Definitive sanctification says: sin's reign is over; growth is the application of an accomplished freedom, not the achievement of one.
usage: Reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God.
The break has been made; live into it.

etymology: From Greek mystikos "hidden" — the unseen real union of believer and Christ.
biblical_def: The real, vital, spiritual joining of every believer to Christ — He in us, we in Him — the ground of all our salvation benefits (John 17:23; Eph 5:32; Col 1:27).
webster_summary: The real spiritual joining of believer to Christ.
webster_full: The hidden but real spiritual union by which the believer is joined to Christ as branch to vine, member to body, bride to bridegroom — the source of justification, sanctification, glorification.
scriptures: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one.
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
Christ in you, the hope of glory.
corruption_summary: Either mocked as fuzzy mysticism or replaced by transactional language that loses the relational depth.
corruption_paragraphs: Mystical here means hidden-but-real, not vague. The union is more real than your bones — it is the ontological ground of your every gospel benefit. Lose it and the gospel becomes a paperwork exchange. Keep it and Christianity becomes a marriage.
usage: Live from union, not toward it.
All Christ's benefits flow from the union.

etymology: From Latin spiritualis + unio — joining in the Spirit.
biblical_def: The Holy Spirit's work joining the believer to Christ; another aspect of the one union, emphasizing the Spirit as the bond (1 Cor 6:17; Rom 8:9-11).
webster_summary: The Spirit-wrought joining of believer to Christ.
webster_full: The aspect of union with Christ accomplished and maintained by the Holy Spirit; He who indwells the believer is the same Spirit who indwells the risen Christ, making the union real.
scriptures: But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body... and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.
corruption_summary: Severed from the doctrine of the Holy Spirit so the union becomes vague mood rather than concrete bond.
corruption_paragraphs: The union is not magic, not metaphor, not feeling — it is the Holy Spirit Himself making one what was two. Recover the doctrine of the Spirit and union becomes solid; lose it and union becomes sentimental.
usage: The Spirit is the bond of our union.
Walk in the Spirit; you walk in union.

etymology: Latin forensis "of the forum" — pertaining to the law-court.
biblical_def: The Reformation doctrine that justification is a legal verdict — God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ's imputed righteousness, not because the sinner has been made internally righteous (Rom 4:5; 5:1).
webster_summary: Justification as legal declaration, not internal change.
webster_full: The Protestant doctrine that justification is a courtroom act in which God, the judge, declares the believing sinner righteous on the basis of Christ's righteousness imputed — distinguished from the internal renewal of sanctification.
scriptures: But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
corruption_summary: Conflated with sanctification by Roman Catholic and 'New Perspective' readings, dissolving the courtroom verdict.
corruption_paragraphs: Forensic justification is not a quirk — it is the gospel. The verdict comes first; the renewal follows. To collapse the two is to lose the assurance the gospel gives the worst sinner. The sinner is justified the moment he believes, not when he has improved enough.
usage: The verdict is in: justified by faith.
Forensic first, then transformative.

etymology: Reformed dogmatic term — Christ's positive law-keeping reckoned to believers.
biblical_def: Christ's perfect, lifelong obedience to the law of God on behalf of His people, imputed to them as their righteousness (Rom 5:19; Phil 2:8).
webster_summary: Christ's perfect law-keeping credited to us.
webster_full: The Reformed term for Christ's positive obedience — His perfect fulfillment of the law throughout His earthly life — reckoned to believers as their own righteousness; complementary to His passive obedience on the cross.
scriptures: For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
Being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law.
corruption_summary: Eclipsed by exclusive focus on the cross, missing the 33 years of perfect law-keeping that grounds our righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The cross is not the only place we needed Christ. He had to live for us as well as die for us — perfectly keeping the law we couldn't keep. Drop active obedience and the gospel only forgives; keep it and the gospel also clothes.
usage: Christ's life clothes you; Christ's death cleanses you.
Active and passive obedience together complete the gospel.

etymology: Reformed dogmatic term — Christ's submission to suffering and death on behalf of His people.
biblical_def: Christ's submission to the curse of the law and the wrath of God in His suffering and death, bearing the penalty due His people (Isa 53:5; Gal 3:13).
webster_summary: Christ's suffering and death credited to us.
webster_full: The Reformed term for Christ's submission to suffering and the cross — bearing the law's penalty for His people; complementary to His active obedience that fulfilled the law's demand.
scriptures: He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a single act on the cross instead of seen as the climax of a willingly-borne lifelong burden.
corruption_paragraphs: 'Passive' here is from the Latin patior — to suffer — not 'inactive.' Christ's passive obedience is His willingness to suffer the curse for His people, climaxing at Calvary but threading through His whole life of grief and rejection.
usage: Christ's death pays your debt.
Active and passive obedience together complete the gospel.

etymology: Reformed shorthand for the five points often summarized by TULIP.
biblical_def: The Reformed cluster confessing total depravity, unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints — together a sovereign-grace soteriology.
webster_summary: Reformed five-point sovereign-grace theology.
webster_full: A common shorthand for the Reformed soteriological cluster: humanity's total depravity, God's unconditional election, Christ's particular atonement, the Spirit's effectual call, and the saints' final perseverance.
scriptures: So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: Caricatured as cold determinism rather than received as the deepest possible exaltation of divine mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrines of grace are not theological math — they are the songs of those who know they would have chosen darkness if grace had not chosen them first. They produce humility, gratitude, and prayer, not pride.
usage: Hold the doctrines of grace humbly.
They are doxology, not dispute.

etymology: Reformed dogmatic term — the saving grace given to the elect.
biblical_def: The saving, regenerating, sanctifying grace given by God only to His elect, distinguished from the common grace shown to all (Eph 2:8-9; 2 Tim 1:9).
webster_summary: Saving grace given only to the elect.
webster_full: The grace by which God effectually saves, regenerates, justifies, and sanctifies His elect; distinguished from common grace which restrains evil and bestows blessings on all without saving.
scriptures: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration.
corruption_summary: Conflated with common grace, blurring why some are saved and others not.
corruption_paragraphs: Common grace falls on all; special grace falls on the elect. The first explains why the unbeliever still has good things; the second explains why the believer is saved. Distinguishing them rightly preserves both compassion for the world and gratitude for salvation.
usage: Special grace saves; common grace restrains.
Both are real; only one regenerates.

etymology: From Latin gratia + salvare "to save."
biblical_def: The grace of God in Christ that actually delivers sinners from condemnation and brings them to glory — not mere divine favor but redemptive power (Eph 2:5-8; Titus 2:11).
webster_summary: Grace that actually saves.
webster_full: The redemptive grace of God which not only inclines Him toward sinners but accomplishes their salvation — calling, regenerating, justifying, sanctifying, and finally glorifying them.
scriptures: Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved).
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.
But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.
corruption_summary: Sentimentalized as God's general goodwill, severed from its specific saving accomplishment.
corruption_paragraphs: Saving grace does not 'try to save' — it saves. It is not divine encouragement but divine power. When Scripture calls grace 'saving,' it is naming what it accomplishes, not what it offers.
usage: Saving grace saves — it does not merely offer.
Walk in the grace that found you.

etymology: Theory of atonement traced to Peter Abelard (12th century).
biblical_def: The atonement theory teaching that Christ's death moves us morally — primarily a demonstration of God's love that softens our hearts to repent — without addressing divine wrath or law-penalty. Insufficient by itself.
webster_summary: Atonement as moral example, not penalty payment.
webster_full: A theory of the atonement holding that Christ's death changes humans by exhibiting divine love that wins them to repentance, but without paying a debt or appeasing wrath. Held alongside other theories it has truth; held alone it loses the gospel.
scriptures: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
Without shedding of blood is no remission.
corruption_summary: Held as the only or primary theory, dropping the propitiation, substitution, and ransom Scripture clearly teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's death IS a moral influence — it really does move us. But it is not only that. To make moral influence the whole of atonement is to leave wrath unaddressed and the law unsatisfied. The cross is a multi-faceted gem; do not grind off all but one face.
usage: The cross does move us — but it does more.
Hold moral influence with substitution.

etymology: Atonement theory developed by Hugo Grotius (17th century).
biblical_def: The atonement theory that Christ's death is a public demonstration of God's hatred of sin upholding moral government, rather than a personal penalty paid for individual sinners. Falls short of penal substitution.
webster_summary: Atonement as public moral-government display.
webster_full: A theory of the atonement, traced to Hugo Grotius, holding that Christ's death is a token suffering by which God upholds moral government and discourages sin, without being a precise payment of penalty for elect sinners.
scriptures: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness... that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.
corruption_summary: Mistaken for penal substitution; differs in that no actual penalty is paid for actual sins.
corruption_paragraphs: Governmental theory keeps the language of penalty but loses its substance. The cross becomes a deterrent, not a payment. Scripture insists Christ bore our sins, not a generic display of disapproval. The substance matters.
usage: Hold the cross as substitution, not just demonstration.
Grotius is a step toward, not the goal.

etymology: Term for the historic Christian doctrine of God shared by Augustine, Aquinas, the Reformers, and the Puritans.
biblical_def: The historic Christian doctrine of God: simple, eternal, immutable, impassible, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, aseity, perfect — distinguished from modern revisions that compromise these attributes.
webster_summary: The historic Christian doctrine of God.
webster_full: The doctrine of God carried through Scripture and the historic creeds — simple, eternal, immutable, impassible, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-present, self-existent, perfect. Held by Athanasius, Augustine, Aquinas, the Reformers, the Puritans, the Westminster divines, and the orthodox today.
scriptures: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM.
For I am the LORD, I change not.
The blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto.
corruption_summary: Dismissed as Greek philosophical baggage rather than the careful articulation of biblical revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern theology often presents classical theism as Hellenistic intrusion. The Fathers and Reformers presented it as careful biblical synthesis. Open theism, process theism, and 'theistic mutualism' are the alternatives — and they each diminish God to make Him manageable.
roots_summary: Greek theos + classical (received) — God of the historic confession.
usage: Recover classical theism for high worship.
The God of Athanasius is the God of Scripture.

etymology: From Latin processio — the Spirit's eternal coming-forth.
biblical_def: The orthodox doctrine that the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father (and the Son, in Western theology) — not by creation but as the third Person's eternal mode of existence (John 15:26).
webster_summary: The Spirit's eternal coming-forth from the Father.
webster_full: The orthodox Trinitarian doctrine that the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father — the Western tradition adding from the Son also (filioque) — distinguished from the Son's eternal generation.
scriptures: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.
But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things.
He breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a creedal trivia point instead of received as real Trinitarian doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Eternal procession is not a footnote — it is the Spirit's eternal personal identity. Take it away and the Trinity collapses into modes. Hold it and worship grows fuller: we adore three Persons, eternally distinct in their relations of origin.
usage: The Spirit eternally proceeds; the Son eternally is begotten.
Trinity in eternal relation, not historical sequence.

etymology: Heresy attributed to Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople (5th century); condemned at Ephesus (431).
biblical_def: The Christological heresy that Christ is two persons (one divine, one human) loosely joined — denying the personal unity of the incarnate Son. Refuted by Cyril of Alexandria.
webster_summary: Heresy of two-persons Christology.
webster_full: The Christological heresy taught by Nestorius that the divine and human in Christ amount to two persons in conjunction rather than one Person with two natures. Condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431.
scriptures: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant.
Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.
corruption_summary: Surfaces today whenever speakers describe 'the human Jesus' as if there were a separable Jesus apart from the divine Son.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech often slips into Nestorianism — 'the human Jesus suffered, but God can't suffer' — splitting Christ into two persons. Chalcedon settles it: one Person, two natures. Without confusion, without separation.
usage: Speak of the one Christ in two natures.
Nestorius split what God joined.

etymology: Heresy attributed to Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople (5th century); condemned at Chalcedon (451).
biblical_def: The Christological heresy that Christ's human nature was absorbed into His divine nature so He has effectively one (mixed) nature — the opposite error of Nestorianism. Refuted at Chalcedon.
webster_summary: Heresy of one-mixed-nature Christology.
webster_full: The Christological heresy that Christ has but one nature, His humanity having been absorbed by or fused with His divinity; condemned at Chalcedon in 451.
scriptures: Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren.
We have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Surfaces today wherever Christ's full humanity is downplayed in favor of His divinity, leaving Him alien to us.
corruption_paragraphs: Eutyches wanted to honor Christ's deity — but at the cost of His humanity. Chalcedon insists: full deity, full humanity, one Person, no mixture. Lose either nature and you lose the Mediator who shares both.
usage: Christ is fully God and fully man, no mixture.
Eutyches melted what God maintained distinct.

etymology: From Augustine of Hippo (354-430), the great African theologian.
biblical_def: The theological tradition flowing from Augustine — original sin, total inability, sovereign grace, predestination, perseverance — taken up by the Reformers as the deepest Western reading of grace.
webster_summary: Augustine's grace-and-sovereignty theology.
webster_full: The theological tradition deriving from Augustine: humanity's bondage to original sin and total inability, salvation by sovereign grace alone, the predestining purpose of God, and the perseverance of the elect. Foundation of Reformed theology.
scriptures: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin... for that all have sinned.
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
corruption_summary: Caricatured as fatalism rather than received as the deepest articulation of grace's priority.
corruption_paragraphs: Augustine fought Pelagius in the 5th century; the Reformers fought a return to Pelagianism in the 16th. The fight is perpetual because man's heart wants to contribute to his salvation. Augustinianism keeps grace at the bottom of the stack.
usage: Augustine's grace is the gospel's grace.
Pelagianism dies hard; Augustinianism revives often.

etymology: From Faustus Socinus (1539-1604), Italian-Polish anti-Trinitarian theologian.
biblical_def: The 16th-17th century rationalist heresy denying the Trinity, the deity of Christ, original sin, and substitutionary atonement; ancestor of modern Unitarianism.
webster_summary: Anti-Trinitarian rationalist heresy of the 16-17th c.
webster_full: The rationalist anti-Trinitarian movement led by Faustus Socinus, denying the Trinity, the deity of Christ, original sin, and substitutionary atonement. The chief Reformation-era opponent against whom Reformed orthodoxy sharpened its doctrine; ancestor of Unitarianism.
scriptures: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
By one man sin entered into the world.
corruption_summary: Recurring under new names — Unitarianism, modernist liberalism, certain progressive Christianities — wherever Trinitarian and substitutionary truths are dismissed as outdated.
corruption_paragraphs: Socinianism is what reason without revelation produces: a Jesus without deity, a humanity without fall, a cross without substitution. The Owen-Socinus debates are still readable; the issues haven't changed.
usage: Socinianism is the perpetual rationalist temptation.
Read John Owen's response.

etymology: Greek homoi-ousios (ὁμοιούσιος) — "of similar substance."
biblical_def: The 4th-century semi-Arian compromise term: the Son is of like substance with the Father, not of the same substance — rejected by Athanasius and the Nicene party in favor of homoousios.
webster_summary: Semi-Arian compromise: like substance, not same.
webster_full: The 4th-century compromise term differing from the Nicene homoousios by a single iota (similar rather than same substance) — rejected because 'similar' falls short of full deity for the Son.
scriptures: I and my Father are one.
Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.
He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
corruption_summary: The proverbial 'iota's worth of difference' that modern observers think is trivial — but isn't.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase 'an iota's difference' comes from this debate. The single Greek letter separates orthodoxy (same substance) from heresy (similar substance). One letter; one Savior or none. Doctrine matters.
usage: Homoousios, not homoiousion — same, not similar.
An iota of doctrine matters.

etymology: Term for the post-Nicene compromise position softening Arianism without embracing Nicaea.
biblical_def: The 4th-century midstream party who rejected pure Arianism (Christ is created) but also rejected Nicene homoousios in favor of homoiousion — a softer subordinationism. Defeated at Constantinople (381).
webster_summary: The compromise between Arianism and Nicaea.
webster_full: The 4th-century theological party who shrank from outright Arianism (which made Christ a creature) but also from Nicene homoousios (which made Him fully God in the same substance), holding instead that He was of like substance — homoiousios.
scriptures: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God.
corruption_summary: Common compromise impulse — wanting to honor Christ without quite confessing His full deity. Recurs perpetually.
corruption_paragraphs: Semi-Arianism is the perpetual middle-path temptation: not quite heretical, not quite orthodox, comfortable with both crowds. Nicaea forces a choice; Constantinople (381) closes the door on the middle. Christ is fully God or He is not God.
usage: The middle is not safer than orthodoxy.
Semi-Arianism is Arianism with manners.

etymology: Term used by open theists for their revision of God's knowledge.
biblical_def: The open-theist proposal that God knows everything that can be known but the future free actions of creatures cannot be known by anyone — denying God's exhaustive foreknowledge. Departs from classical theism and biblical revelation.
webster_summary: Open theism's denial of exhaustive divine foreknowledge.
webster_full: The open-theist claim that God's omniscience is limited because the future free choices of creatures are not knowable in principle; God knows what is knowable but cannot foreknow free actions. Rejected by classical and Reformed orthodoxy.
scriptures: I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done.
For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.
corruption_summary: Marketed as 'a more relational God' but actually delivers a smaller, less-trustworthy God.
corruption_paragraphs: Limited omniscience is sold as relational warmth — God is surprised, He grows with us. The trade is reduction: a god whose promises depend on prediction is no longer the God who declares the end from the beginning. Smaller God, smaller hope.
usage: Reject limited omniscience; recover the Isaiah-46 God.
He declares the end from the beginning.

etymology: From Latin praevenire "to come before."
biblical_def: Coming before; a Wesleyan theological term for the grace of God that goes before and enables a free response to the gospel — distinguished from the Reformed effectual call. Universal in scope, resistible by design.
webster_summary: Going before; Wesleyan grace that precedes faith.
webster_full: Going before; especially in Arminian-Wesleyan theology, the grace of God which precedes any human response and partially restores ability to respond to the gospel — universal but resistible. The Reformed alternative is the effectual call which is particular and irresistible.
scriptures: That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.
The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance.
corruption_summary: Inflated by some Arminians to do what only the effectual call can do — actually save.
corruption_paragraphs: Prevenient grace is real — God works in every soul before they come. The disagreement is whether that working merely enables response or actually secures it. Wesley says enables; Calvin says (in the elect) secures. Both confess prior grace; the question is its strength.
usage: Prevenient grace prepares the heart.
Wesleyans confess it; Reformed confess effectual call.
